cards.back: A constant: one value shared by every instance, assigned once
cards.extra: static means it belongs to the class; final means it cannot be reassigned. Together they are Java's constant, and convention writes them in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Const { static final int LIMIT = 3; }   // one value, assigned once, shared
class Ex { { System.out.println(new Const().LIMIT + " " + Const.LIMIT); } }

cards.front: When is a static variable initialised?
cards.back: Once, when the class is first loaded — not per object
cards.extra: That is why static state survives between instances and why it is shared. Instance variables get their values per object; statics do not.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Counter { static int count = 1; int id; }   // static initialised once when the class is loaded
class Ex { { System.out.println(new Counter().count + " " + new Counter().count); } }

cards.extra: Math.round returns long even for a float argument, which is why assigning it to an int needs a cast in older code. abs keeps the argument's type.
cards.example:
int a = Math.abs(-5);
long r = Math.round(3.7);
System.out.println(a + " " + r + " " + ((Object) r).getClass().getSimpleName());   // 5 4 Long

cards.back: Generics accept only class and interface types, not primitives
cards.extra: Use ArrayList<Integer>. Autoboxing then lets you add ints directly, so in practice the restriction costs you nothing.
cards.example:
java.util.ArrayList<Integer> ints = new java.util.ArrayList<>();   // Integer, not int
ints.add(3);
// java.util.ArrayList<int> bad = new java.util.ArrayList<>();   // compile error: no primitive type arguments

cards.front: Why does Java separate number formatting from printing?
cards.back: So a formatted String can go anywhere — a GUI field, a table, a log — not just stdout
cards.extra: Formatting into a String first, then displaying it, keeps the two concerns apart. That is what String.format buys you over printf.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String text = String.format("%,d", 1234567);   // formatting makes a String
System.out.println(text);   // it can also go to a GUI field, a table or a log
new javax.swing.JLabel(text);

cards.front: In String.format("%.2f", 3.14159), what does each part mean?
cards.back: % starts the specifier; .2 is precision (2 decimals); f is the conversion
cards.extra: The result is "3.14" — rounded, not truncated. Drop the precision and you get the full default representation.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = String.format("%.2f", 3.14159);
System.out.println(s);   // 3.14: % starts, .2 is precision (2 decimals), f is the conversion

cards.front: Which part of a format specifier is mandatory?
cards.back: The conversion — the letter that says how to read the argument
cards.extra: d integer, f floating point, s string, x hex. Flags, width and precision are all optional extras.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = String.format("%d", 42);   // d is the mandatory conversion
System.out.println(s);   // 42

cards.front: How do you print 1234567 with grouping separators?
cards.extra: The comma flag is locale-sensitive, so on a German JVM you get dots. That is correct behaviour, not a bug.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods

cards.front: What does import static java.lang.Math.*; let you do?
cards.extra: It imports static members rather than a class. Handy for constants and maths, but it hides where a method comes from — use sparingly.
cards.example:
import static java.lang.Math.*;
class Ex {
  static void m() { System.out.println(round(3.7f) + " " + abs(-5)); }   // 4 5, no Math. prefix
}

cards.front: You must hand an int to code that only accepts an Object. What do you do?
cards.extra: Primitives are not objects, so they cannot go where Object is expected. The wrapper is a real heap object holding the value, which is also why a collection of Integers costs more memory than an int[].
cards.example:
Object boxed = Integer.valueOf(3);   // wrap the int for code that needs an Object
Object auto = 3;   // autoboxing does the same
System.out.println(boxed + " " + auto);

cards.front: Two % specifiers, three arguments in String.format. What happens?
cards.back: The extra argument is ignored — no exception
cards.extra: Too few arguments throws (MissingFormatArgumentException); too many are silently dropped. One more reason to format with a specifier you can count.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = String.format("%d %d", 1, 2, 3);
System.out.println(s);   // 1 2: the extra argument is ignored, no exception
